LANG_PRIOR_quote: While the Elamite language has been suggested as the language of the Proto-Elamite inscriptions, there is no positive evidence of this.
VALUES_quote: This is because certain signs, notably a majority of the numerical signs, are similar to the neighboring Mesopotamian proto-cuneiform.
notes: Conflict: Mnamon says "It is assumed that the language recorded by this script is an ancient form of Elamite."; coded from Wikipedia. CORPUS NS: about 1600 tablets (Mnamon: over 1,700 texts), no typical length.

LANG_PRIOR_quote: According to common theory, Canaanites or Hyksos who spoke a Canaanite language repurposed Egyptian hieroglyphs to construct a different script.
ANCHOR_quote: Likewise, this allowed another recurring word mʿhbʿlt to be translated as "Beloved of (the) Lady", a reading which became very acceptable after the lemma was found carved underneath a hieroglyphic inscription which read "Beloved of Hathor, Lady of Turquoise".
VALUES_quote: Ten years later, in 1916, Alan Gardiner, one of the premier Egyptologists of the early and mid-20th century, published his own interpretation of Petrie's findings, arguing that the glyphs appeared to be early versions of the signs used for later Semitic languages such as Phoenician, and was able to assign sound values and reconstructed names to some of the letters by assuming they represented what would later become the common Semitic abjad.
WORDDIV_quote: The poor conservation of the inscriptions, their brevity and the absence of separation marks between two grammatical units all strongly penalize decipherment.
notes: ANCHOR 2: a hieroglyphic inscription "Beloved of Hathor, Lady of Turquoise" over the matching Proto-Sinaitic word; the Hathor temple setting also gives an expected name. CORPUS: 30 to 40 inscriptions, some of 3 or 4 signs and some longer, with no typical length, so NS.

LANG_PRIOR_quote: There are three serious obstacles to decipherment, assuming rongorongo is truly writing: the small number of remaining texts, the lack of context such as illustrations in which to interpret them, and the poor attestation of the Old Rapa Nui language, since modern Rapa Nui is heavily mixed with Tahitian and is therefore unlikely to closely reflect the language of the tablets.
ANCHOR_quote: A list of the glyphs they identified was published posthumously, along with a complete account of the chants for A and B.

CORPUS_quote: The 26 rongorongo texts with letter codes are inscribed on wooden objects, each with between 2 and 2320 simple glyphs and components of compound glyphs, for over 15,000 in all.
notes: ANCHOR: coded 2 because the Jaussen list (glyphs glossed by Metoro) counts as a glossary. The account says it "has not led to an understanding of the script" and also cites "the lack of ... parallel texts which can be read"; a coder who does not count the Jaussen list would code 0. WORDDIV: the Santiago Staff alone has 103 vertical lines, which divide sections, not words. CORPUS: page 2 gives "only 15,000 legible glyphs".

LANG_HIND_quote: Safaitic (Arabic: ٱلصَّفَائِيَّة Al-Ṣafāʾiyyah) is a variety of the South Semitic scripts that was used by the Arabs in southern Syria and northern Jordan in the Ḥarrah region, to carve rock inscriptions in various dialects of Old Arabic and Ancient North Arabian.
WORDDIV_quote: The inscriptions can be written in nearly any direction and there are no word dividers.
notes: LANG_PRIOR: the "traditional view" (Ancient North Arabian, not Arabic proper) is undated, so nothing places a language identification at 1901. CORPUS: about 30,000 inscriptions (Wikipedia) or about 35,000 graffiti (Mnamon), but neither account gives a typical length, so no token figure can be computed; at least C by count alone. The two counts differ.

CORPUS: inscriptions of up to ten to twelve syllables, but no count of inscriptions.
